on_orangeman_wall.blurb: A clean little wall within the Bluffs, a city park on the north edge of Thunder Bay. It holds about a dozen lines and variations, split evenly between top-rope and gear-protected trad, from a scramble-level start through easy fifth class up to a handful of stiff 5.11 problems. The bulk of the climbing sits between 5.5 and 5.9, so it suits beginners, instructors and anyone setting up a relaxed day on the rope. Routes are short and anchors are bolted at the clifftop. You reach it by walking along the bluff top, then rappelling in or continuing to a ravine that can be muddy.

on_9l_headspace_wall.blurb: The first cliff you meet when the trail along the Lion's Head escarpment on the Bruce Peninsula reaches the edge. Most of the sixteen lines are bolted sport routes, with a few trad lines, and the grade range is weighted toward the hard end: a scattering of 5.10s, then a solid block of 5.11 and 5.12 climbs and a few 5.13s, with almost nothing easy. Because you arrive from the top, you rappel in, and some lines have hanging belays reached from the rim. Expect a committed first visit on complicated terrain.

on_jones_road_cliff_aka_jones_rhode.blurb: A roadside crag in forest and small-lake country on the Canadian Shield, north of Kenora in northwestern Ontario. Routes run roughly 20 to 100 feet and mix cracks, faces, slabs, chimneys and a few overhangs on solid rock. Most of the sixteen lines here are bolted sport climbs with a few trad ones, and the difficulty clusters in the 5.9 to 5.11 range, with the largest group at 5.11. Boulders along the highway and on big detached blocks add problems from easy to V4. The base is only a short scramble from the cars, trails run along the foot of the cliff, and a quiet lake is a five-minute walk away.
on_jones_road_cliff_aka_jones_rhode.parking_note: Drive about 30 km up Highway 671 from the Kenora bypass; a sandy pull-off sits right below the cliff, which rises on the road's west side.

on_3_ice_palace.blurb: A compact ice and mixed zone in Orient Bay on the north shore of Lake Superior, hidden from the highway yet packed with good lines. The fifteen climbs are mostly water ice from WI2 up to WI5, plus mixed routes reaching M8, with some of the best-known lines at WI4 and WI5. Most faces look west to northwest, so sun does little until well into March. The walk from the road takes around 10 minutes to the north end and roughly 20 to the south end. It is popular, but there is normally something free to climb.

on_bizzaro_world.blurb: A boulder zone in the wooded Niagara Glen, near the Niagara River gorge, north of the Nature Centre. The setting is shady and cool even in summer, and the trails wander enough that getting turned around is common. The problems here are mostly friendly: a spread from VB through V4 with a few of each grade, then and a pair of much harder V7 problems. Expect polished holds on popular lines and grades that feel inconsistent. The way in runs down a large metal staircase toward the river and then along a red trail.
